account: In Sadhan Haldar v NCT of Delhi, the Delhi High Court had pressed the police to test-run facial recognition. The Ministry of Women and Child Development then supplied data on about seven lakh missing children from the Track Child portal. The Wire cites the Bureau of Police Research and Development's Compendium of Equipment, which records that the police bought two facial recognition systems on 28 March 2018. Innefu Labs manufactured them, and Pelorus Technologies supplied them. On 22 April 2018 the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported in Business Standard on an affidavit from the ministry to the Delhi High Court. It said that the Delhi Police, “on a trial basis, used the FRS on 45,000 children living in different children's homes”. It added that 2,930 children “could be recognised between April 6 and April 10”. The ministry's secretary Rakesh Srivastava said that the police shared the outcome on 10 April. The same report says that identities “have been established and efforts are on to help them reunite with their families”. On 23 August 2018 Delhi Police counsel Rahul Mehra told the High Court: “The software is not good. There is only two per cent match” (NDTV). That was in a habeas corpus matter about women missing from a placement agency. On 22 January 2019 the High Court (Hima Kohli and Manoj Kumar Ohri JJ) recorded in Sadhan Haldar what it was told. The software “has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far”, against 5,160 children untraced out of 19,916 reported missing in 2016–2018. On 23 August 2019 the ministry's counsel told the Delhi High Court that the software sometimes matched photographs of missing boys with girls. The court had asked why fewer than 1 percent of children were matched. It ordered the ministry to chart each identified child and the status of the child's return home (PTI, 24 August 2019). A Centre for Internet and Society (CIS India) report gives 10,617 matches, of which 3,202 identities were verified, and no reunification count. On 2 and 3 July 2025 the Pulitzer Center republished The Wire's investigations. They quote an Innefu blog that claims that its AI Vision product “helped in identifying 3000 missing children” in its first four days. No reunification is documented in any cited source.

ai_role.statement: The software produced the 2,930 matches reported in the ministry's affidavit. The claim rests on the police's report of raw output, relayed by PTI, and on the vendor's blog. No cited source verifies a single match to a reunification. The police counsel described the match rate as two percent in August 2018. The Delhi High Court recorded in January 2019 that the software had not helped crack any case. The CIS India figures (10,617 matches, 3,202 identities verified) come from a report that is not among the sources.

fields.account: In Sadhan Haldar v NCT of Delhi, the Delhi High Court had pressed the police to test-run facial recognition. The Ministry of Women and Child Development then supplied data on about seven lakh missing children from the Track Child portal. The Wire cites the Bureau of Police Research and Development's Compendium of Equipment, which records that the police bought two facial recognition systems on 28 March 2018. Innefu Labs manufactured them, and Pelorus Technologies supplied them. On 22 April 2018 the Press Trust of India (PTI) reported in Business Standard on an affidavit from the ministry to the Delhi High Court. It said that the Delhi Police, “on a trial basis, used the FRS on 45,000 children living in different children's homes”. It added that 2,930 children “could be recognised between April 6 and April 10”. The ministry's secretary Rakesh Srivastava said that the police shared the outcome on 10 April. The same report says that identities “have been established and efforts are on to help them reunite with their families”. On 23 August 2018 Delhi Police counsel Rahul Mehra told the High Court: “The software is not good. There is only two per cent match” (NDTV). That was in a habeas corpus matter about women missing from a placement agency. On 22 January 2019 the High Court (Hima Kohli and Manoj Kumar Ohri JJ) recorded in Sadhan Haldar what it was told. The software “has not helped in cracking any case of missing children so far”, against 5,160 children untraced out of 19,916 reported missing in 2016–2018. On 23 August 2019 the ministry's counsel told the Delhi High Court that the software sometimes matched photographs of missing boys with girls. The court had asked why fewer than 1 percent of children were matched. It ordered the ministry to chart each identified child and the status of the child's return home (PTI, 24 August 2019). A Centre for Internet and Society (CIS India) report gives 10,617 matches, of which 3,202 identities were verified, and no reunification count. On 2 and 3 July 2025 the Pulitzer Center republished The Wire's investigations. They quote an Innefu blog that claims that its AI Vision product “helped in identifying 3000 missing children” in its first four days. No reunification is documented in any cited source.
